statement: Five houses stand in a row. Each house is painted one of 3 colours, and any two houses next to each other must be different colours. In how many different ways can the row be painted?

choices.misconception: I multiplied $3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2$ and missed one of the five houses.
I gave every house 2 choices, $2^5$, forgetting that the first house can be any of the 3 colours.
I added the choices, $3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2$, instead of multiplying them.
I ignored the rule about neighbours and counted $3^5$ ways.

hints: Paint the houses one at a time, from left to right.
The multiplication principle: count the colour choices for each house in turn, given the house just before it, then multiply, because all the choices happen together.
The first house has 3 choices. Every later house only has to differ from the house on its left, so it has 2 choices.

solutions.reliable: Paint from left to right. The first house can be any of 3 colours. Each later house must differ from its left neighbour, which leaves 2 choices whatever happened before. So there are $3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 48$ ways. The transferable idea: when choices are made one after another and the number of options at each step is fixed, multiply.
solutions.elegant: Check with small cases: 2 houses give $3 \times 2 = 6$ ways, which is easy to list, and each extra house doubles the count, so 5 houses give $6 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 48$.

whyOnTest: Neighbour rules look as if they need casework, but each house only has to avoid one colour, so the multiplication principle applies.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
